item.content:encoded: At the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife 65th anniversary celebration, Dr. Tunji Olowolafe , Founder of the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation (TOF) , called on Nigerian universities to open research to more people, test long-held beliefs with scientific rigour and carry discoveries out of the laboratory and into the economy. Speaking on the theme, Promoting Research Excellence and Innovation in Postgraduate Studies: Charting the Future, Dr. Olowolafe reframed research as the disciplined habit of correcting a nation’s course based on evidence. He described the postgraduate college as the intellectual engine room of a nation, where society sends its sharpest minds to challenge conventional wisdom and demand honest, data-driven answers. His first strategy called for opening the gates of research earlier, wider and more flexibly. He urged OAU to make its Staff Schools benchmarks for Africa, with science, technology and artificial intelligence at the core of the curriculum. He pointed to the Foundation’s Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are-Ekiti, which opened in September 2025 with 100 students and now has more than 170, alongside an ICT centre teaching artificial intelligence, coding, graphic design and Mandarin, with instructors teaching live from Beijing through a Starlink connection. “The postgraduate researchers of 2040 are sitting in primary classrooms today,” he said. He also questioned whether every road to postgraduate research must run through a four-year degree, inviting universities to recognize prior learning and demonstrated expertise without lowering standards. With only about one million of the two million UTME candidates admitted in 2025, he argued that flexible, digital study must become the standard model, since a digital campus needs no physical acreage. This builds on the Foundation’s Project Digi-Teach, which is training academic staff at Ekiti State University (EKSU) for digital proficiency. His second strategy urged researchers to test what society believes. Rather than dismissing indigenous knowledge without investigation or defending it without validation, he called for rigorous testing, citing Chinese scientist Tu Youyou , whose study of a centuries-old herbal remedy produced the malaria treatment artemisinin and a Nobel Prize. He extended the same principle to national history, including sensitive chapters such as the Civil War. “She neither rejected tradition nor accepted it. She tested it,” he said. The third strategy focused on pushing research out of the laboratory and directly into the economy. Dr. Olowolafe advocated university promotion structures that reward patents, commercial products and solved industrial problems alongside traditional journal publications. “Research is complete only when it leaves the laboratory and improves lives,” he said. Pointing to OAU’s exceptional tech pedigree, including Flutterwave and Moniepoint founded by its graduates, he challenged the global alumni community to scale up their financial, institutional and mentorship support for research tenfold. To support this vision, the Foundation will install a solar power system for the Postgraduate College, provide a virtual learning and oral defense facility and modernize the College Boardroom. TOF will also fund pilot studies on a case-by-case basis and sponsor training in grant writing and donor compliance, working with OAU’s Central Office of Research and Advancement Office. “Our ambition must go beyond providing infrastructure to building institutions that can generate knowledge and attract global research funding. By strengthening the capacity of our universities, we can expand opportunities for our people and position Nigeria to compete more effectively in the global knowledge economy,” he added. Through these ideas and commitments, the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation continues to advance its broader ambition of strengthening the institutions, skills and opportunities that support Nigeria’s long-term development. Its work across education, digital learning and research capacity reflects a sustained commitment to equipping institutions and the next generation with the tools to compete and thrive in an increasingly knowledge-driven world. item.title: Google Pay Now Available to Visa Card Holders in Nigeria for Fast, Secure Digital Payments
item.description: Visa , one of the world’s leaders in digital payments, applauds the launch of Google Pay by participating financial institutions in Nigeria, supported through Visa’s partnership with Google . Eligible Visa cardholders of participating financial institutions can now securely add their cards to Google Wallet and make fast, convenient, and secure payments across millions of contactless acceptance points and online merchants. The launch by participating financial institutions marks another significant milestone in Nigeria’s digital payments journey, providing consumers with a simple and secure way to pay using their Android devices. By adding their eligible Visa cards to Google Wallet, users can tap to pay in stores, make purchases online, and enjoy a seamless payment experience across Google’s ecosystem. Google Pay uses tokenization technology to help protect payment information. Instead of storing or sharing a customer’s card number during transactions, a unique digital token is used, providing an additional layer of security while maintaining a fast and convenient checkout experience. As consumer demand for digital-first payment experiences continues to grow, the partnership between Visa and Google, working alongside Nigerian financial institutions, aims to support contactless payment adoption and provide Nigerians with more ways to pay securely wherever Visa contactless payments are accepted. “At Visa, we are committed to advancing the future of payments by delivering innovative, secure, and seamless payment experiences for consumers across Nigeria and beyond . Through our partnership with Google, we are pleased to support our financial institution partners as they bring Google Pay to their cardholders, combining the security of Visa’s global payment network with the convenience consumers increasingly expect in a digital-first world. Helping more people pay with confidence using their mobile devices supports digital commerce, financial inclusion, and the continued growth of Nigeria’s digital economy,” said Andrew Uaboi , Vice President and Cluster Head, Visa West Africa . “We are delighted to bring Google Wallet to Nigeria, a market at the forefront of financial innovation in Africa. Google Wallet makes everyday transactions faster and safer while removing the friction of carrying physical cards. By working alongside Nigeria’s leading financial institutions, we are expanding access to modern digital payment tools for millions of everyday consumers,” said Olumide Balogun , Country Director, Google West Africa About Visa Visa (NYSE: V) is a world leader in digital payments, facilitating transactions between consumers, sellers, financial institutions and government entities across more than 200 countries and territories. Our mission is to connect the world through the most innovative, convenient, reliable, and secure payments network, enabling individuals, businesses, and economies to thrive. item.title: S.E.A CONSULTING Showcases Nigerian Craftsmanship at Design Week Lagos 2026
item.description: At this year’s Design Week Lagos , S.EA.CONSULTING brought its vision to REDESIGN AFRICA to life through an interactive exhibition that invited visitors to touch, listen, explore and connect. Presented at the National Theatre, Lagos, the installation placed local craftsmanship at the centre of a contemporary African living experience. Deep burgundy surfaces, raw tree bark, sculptural textures and a contemporary sofa from S.EA.HOMES created a setting shaped by Nigerian culture and heritage. Finishing materials were served on a dark hardwood table supported by clear acrylic bases, giving the illusion of floating wood. Guests could handle samples and discover the possibilities behind the finished spaces. Wireless headphones offered a choice of music and the founder’s statement, while a digital screen introduced the firm’s services, products, and projects. An in-house photographer captured visitors engaging with the installation, making their presence part of its story. Through this approach, S.EA.CONSULTING made a clear statement: African exhibitions should give local makers, materials and ways of living a central role. Cultural heritage offers a foundation for contemporary design that meets global standards of quality, functionality and execution. The experience connected interior architecture with sourcing, craftsmanship and everyday life, demonstrating how collaboration transforms individual products into spaces with meaning. For S.EA.CONSULTING, showing the world how we live begins with recognising the value of what we make, the stories we carry and the hands that bring our ideas to life. Rooted in culture. Built through collaboration. REDESIGN AFRICA. Wireless headphones offered a choice of music and the founder’s statement, while a digital screen introduced the firm’s services, products, and projects. An in-house photographer captured visitors engaging with the installation, making their presence part of its story. Through this approach, S.EA.CONSULTING made a clear statement: African exhibitions should give local makers, materials and ways of living a central role. Cultural heritage offers a foundation for contemporary design that meets global standards of quality, functionality and execution. The experience connected interior architecture with sourcing, craftsmanship and everyday life, demonstrating how collaboration transforms individual products into spaces with meaning. For S.EA.CONSULTING, showing the world how we live begins with recognising the value of what we make, the stories we carry and the hands that bring our ideas to life. Rooted in culture. Built through collaboration. REDESIGN AFRICA. item.title: Eko Hotels at 50: A Defining Moment for African Hospitality on the Global Stage
item.description: The Legacy Gala & Awards night : Fifty Years of Building More Than a Hotel. Fifty Years of Building a Nation’s Hospitality Identity. 2nd of October 2026 was written in the sands of time, because some hotels are built to accommodate history, others are built to make it. For fifty years, Eko Hotels & Suites has done both. Beneath the lights of an extraordinary golden jubilee celebration, one of Africa’s most recognisable hospitality institutions made a statement that extended far beyond the walls of the magnificent Eko Convention Centre . Africa does not lack the capacity to deliver world-class excellence. What it needs are more institutions courageous enough to demonstrate it. The occasion was The Legacy Gala & Awards night, the grand celebration marking fifty years of Eko Hotels & Suites. An evening of African grandeur, international entertainment, cultural pride, distinguished personalities and extraordinary hospitality. But to describe it simply as a glamorous anniversary celebration would be to misunderstand its significance. This was not merely a party, It was fifty years of enterprise taking a bow, Fifty years of memories finding their voices, Fifty years of an institution reminding a continent that excellence is not foreign to Africa a nd for one unforgettable evening, history took attendance. A Hotel Became Part of a Nation’s Story There are buildings that occupy space, and there are institutions that occupy memory, Eko Hotels & Suites belongs to the latter. Across five decades, its corridors have welcomed presidents and policymakers, entrepreneurs and entertainers, diplomats and dreamers, international visitors and generations of Nigerian families. Within its halls, businesses have been negotiated, friendships formed, cultures celebrated, careers launched and milestones immortalized. For many, Eko Hotels is where Lagos welcomes the world, f or others, it is where the world first encounters the warmth, ambition, sophistication and extraordinary possibilities of Lagos. Yet perhaps its greatest achievement is not simply that it has remained standing for fifty years. It is that it has remained RELEVANT. Eko Hotels has consistently demonstrated that hospitality must evolve beyond accommodation, It must become an experience, a cultural encounter, a n economic opportunity, a reason to travel and reason to return. Because the greatest hotels do not merely sell rooms. They give destinations a reputation worth travelling for. item.content:encoded: The Legacy Gala & Awards night : Fifty Years of Building More Than a Hotel. Fifty Years of Building a Nation’s Hospitality Identity. 2nd of October 2026 was written in the sands of time, because some hotels are built to accommodate history, others are built to make it. For fifty years, Eko Hotels & Suites has done both. Beneath the lights of an extraordinary golden jubilee celebration, one of Africa’s most recognisable hospitality institutions made a statement that extended far beyond the walls of the magnificent Eko Convention Centre . Africa does not lack the capacity to deliver world-class excellence. What it needs are more institutions courageous enough to demonstrate it. The occasion was The Legacy Gala & Awards night, the grand celebration marking fifty years of Eko Hotels & Suites. An evening of African grandeur, international entertainment, cultural pride, distinguished personalities and extraordinary hospitality. But to describe it simply as a glamorous anniversary celebration would be to misunderstand its significance. This was not merely a party, It was fifty years of enterprise taking a bow, Fifty years of memories finding their voices, Fifty years of an institution reminding a continent that excellence is not foreign to Africa a nd for one unforgettable evening, history took attendance. A Hotel Became Part of a Nation’s Story There are buildings that occupy space, and there are institutions that occupy memory, Eko Hotels & Suites belongs to the latter. Across five decades, its corridors have welcomed presidents and policymakers, entrepreneurs and entertainers, diplomats and dreamers, international visitors and generations of Nigerian families. Within its halls, businesses have been negotiated, friendships formed, cultures celebrated, careers launched and milestones immortalized. For many, Eko Hotels is where Lagos welcomes the world, f or others, it is where the world first encounters the warmth, ambition, sophistication and extraordinary possibilities of Lagos. Yet perhaps its greatest achievement is not simply that it has remained standing for fifty years. It is that it has remained RELEVANT. In a world where brands disappear as quickly as trends emerge, longevity is an achievement. But longevity accompanied by reinvention is leadership. Eko Hotels has consistently demonstrated that hospitality must evolve beyond accommodation, It must become an experience, a cultural encounter, a n economic opportunity, a reason to travel and reason to return. Because the greatest hotels do not merely sell rooms. They give destinations a reputation worth travelling for. The Night Africa Wore Her Crown The Legacy Gala & Awards night brought together more than 1,000 distinguished guests, representing an extraordinary convergence of business, government, entertainment, culture and society. Among the dignitaries were Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu , Deputy Governor Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat , prominent business leaders, industry executives, celebrities and long-standing friends of the institution. It was a gathering that reflected not simply the prestige of a hotel, but the depth of relationships cultivated across generations. The evening’s entertainment brought together internationally celebrated musician Wyclef Jean and Nigerian highlife sensation Flavour , creating a memorable meeting of African and Caribbean musical heritage. Music, fashion, theatrical expression and celebration converged in a spectacle befitting the occasion. Yet, beyond the performances lay a more compelling message. African creativity is not a decorative addition to hospitality. It is one of it’s greatest competitive advantages. Africa’s music travels the world, African fashion influences global runways, African cuisine carries the memory of generations, African storytelling continues to captivate audiences far beyond our borders and, many started on Eko Hotels grounds. The question is no longer whether Africa possesses what the world desires, t he question is whether we are sufficiently intentional about converting these cultural assets into sustainable industries, jobs, investments and compelling destination experiences. At The Gala, Eko Hotels offered its own answer. Africa need not borrow another continent’s identity to earn the world’s admiration. She need only invest boldly enough in her own. There is, however, another story that deserves equal billing. It is the story of the people, n ot the famous faces photographed beneath the lights, n ot the glittering personalities whose arrival commands applause b ut the extraordinary men and women whose daily dedication has sustained Eko Hotels for half a century. The housekeepers who prepare rooms with meticulous care, t he waiters who understand that genuine service is an act of dignity, t he engineers who keep an enormous hospitality operation functioning, the security personnel who protect its people and promises, t he gardeners, technicians, stewards, reservation officers, accountants, sales professionals, event planners, administrative teams and countless others whose contributions rarely make newspaper headlines. These are the custodians of the brand. The quiet architects of its reputation and t he human infrastructure behind its commercial success. For fifty years, generations of employees have given their skills, energy, creativity and commitment to an institution that has become part of Nigeria’s hospitality heritage. Their stories may not always appear in annual reports, but their fingerprints are everywhere. A hotel may be built with concrete, steel and capital. But a legacy is built with people who choose, every day, to care. The Chairman, Christopher Chagoury boldly said in an interview. Perhaps, this is one of the most important lessons of Eko Hotels at fifty: buildings can be replicated, interiors redesigned and technology acquired, but a culture of excellence must be nurtured and that culture is ultimately human. The Leadership understands the weight of the legacy. Behind every enduring institution is a succession of decisions, investments, sacrifices and moments when leadership chooses long-term value over immediate convenience. The golden jubilee provided an opportunity to recognize the vision and stewardship that have guided Eko Hotels through five decades. Under the leadership of their Managing Director, Ghassan Faddoul , General Manager Danny Kioupouroglou and the wider executive management team, the institution continues to strengthen it’s position as a defining hospitality destination. Their collective responsibility extends beyond protecting a celebrated past, to redesigning a future, our past will be proud of, long after we are gone. It is to ensure that the institution remains competitive, innovative and relevant to future generations. The true measure of leadership, after all, is not simply what it achieves during its tenure, i t is what remains valuable long after that tenure has ended. Legacy is not the applause we receive while we are present. It is the relevance of what we build when we are no longer in the room. Fifty years of Eko Hotels is therefore not merely a tribute to endurance, i t is a testament to institutional stewardship. From Hospitality To Destination Economics Perhaps the most consequential chapter in Eko Hotels’ evolution is it’s expanding role in connecting hospitality with tourism, culture, entertainment and the creative economy. Through initiatives such as Tropical Christmas Wonderland, Theatre @ Eko Hotels, Hakuna Matata Theme Park and other destination experiences, the institution has increasingly demonstrated how hospitality infrastructure can become a platform for cultural production and economic participation. These initiatives represent a larger philosophy: a hotel should not wait for tourism demand to arrive. It can actively help create the reasons people travel. item.title: Yinka Ogunbiyi Shows HaloBraid’s Automated Hair-Braiding Technology in New Demo
item.description: Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi, creator of the automated HaloBraid device engineered to complete braids up to five times faster. What if you could get your braids done in a fraction of the usual time and still leave the salon with the style you wanted? A new demonstration of HaloBraid, the automated braiding device created by Nigerian-American engineer and Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi , gives us a closer look at how that could work. Designed to help professional hairdressers braid hair up to five times faster while reducing the physical strain that comes with hours of styling, HaloBraid is now being demonstrated in action. And the interesting part is that the machine doesn’t do everything. The stylist still plays an important role in the process. Here’s how it works. The stylist sections the hair, applies the necessary products and starts the braid by hand before feeding it into the device. HaloBraid then handles the repetitive weaving along the length of the hair, while the stylist returns to finish and seal the ends. This means the machine takes care of a time-consuming part of the process, with the stylist still responsible for creating the final hairstyle. For Yinka, the idea behind HaloBraid comes from a very personal experience. Sharing the story behind the invention, she said: My braid story starts at age four, sitting between my mum’s legs as she braided my hair for the first time. Since then, I’ve spent thousands of hours getting my hair braided — and heard the same story from stylists and clients again and again: braiding is beautiful, but it takes too much time and too much strain. As a biomechanical engineer, I knew there had to be a better way, so we built HaloBraid with stylists from the beginning, bringing together inventors, designers, and builders behind some of the world’s most loved hair and beauty products. HaloBraid was built for my mum, my stylists, my aunties, and people around the world who know what it means to spend hours in the chair. The company has also secured $7 million in seed funding, with the investment round led by Seven Seven Six, the venture capital firm founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian , who is married to tennis champion Serena Williams . With the newly shared demonstration, HaloBraid is showing how its technology works alongside professional stylists, combining hand-braiding techniques with automated weaving to reduce the time and physical effort involved in protective hairstyling. The post Yinka Ogunbiyi Shows HaloBraid’s Automated Hair-Braiding Technology in New Demo appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Adekunle Gold Brings Black-Tie Style & Afrobeats to the Ballon d’Or
item.description: Adekunle Gold en route to the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony in London wearing a double-breasted tuxedo and dark sunglasses. Anywhere you see AG Baby , please tell him to come to the front! This suit is really suiting on him, what! Adekunle Gold stepped out for the 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony at the London Palladium, and we need a minute with this look. The Nigerian singer gave us a black-tie moment in a double-breasted black tuxedo with wide satin peak lapels, a white pleated dress shirt and a black satin bow tie. Simple? Yes. Boring? Absolutely not! Adekunle Gold wearing a tailored double-breasted tuxedo and black patent shoes. The accessories deserve their own appreciation, too. AG Baby pinned a circular brooch with a blue centre stone and textured gold detailing to his lapel, then added dark oval sunglasses, gold hoop earrings, a statement gold ring and a luxury wristwatch with a leather strap. Glossy black patent shoes completed the look, and honestly, we love how the gold details bring a little personality to the classic black-and-white combination. Adekunle Gold adjusting his leather strap wristwatch while wearing a pleated evening shirt and bow tie. But the night wasn’t all about looking good. Adekunle Gold also took the stage at the official Ballon d’Or after-party, performing his hit song “ Party No Dey Stop ” alongside other fan favourites. So, while football’s biggest names gathered in London to celebrate the beautiful game, AG Baby made sure Nigerian music had a place in the festivities, too. Adekunle Gold posing on the red carpet at the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony at the London Palladium. item.title: How Can Africans Advance Cross-Country Equity and Opportunities Through AI?
item.description: Photo source: Goalkeepers 2026 Report For years, Africans have explored how to connect seamlessly without hurdles. As several opportunities are being explored through AI, Africans are also exploring whether AI can be used to advance cross-country opportunities and equity. If it can, what would it look like? What are the initial challenges that can hinder it from happening? What can governments and organisations do to enhance it? Artificial intelligence is changing how people learn, work, build businesses and access information. For young Africans, what opportunities does it present to solve problems, develop new skills and participate in an economy that is becoming increasingly digital? How can those opportunities be available to everyone in the same way? A young person with reliable internet access, a laptop and access to AI training has an advantage over someone who lacks these resources. The gap widens further when we consider young people across countries with different levels of digital infrastructure and investment. If AI is to improve the lives of African youth, access to its benefits must extend beyond the countries and communities already positioned to take advantage of it. African countries need to work together, share resources and invest in solutions that respond to the needs of their people. Bill Gates in Rwanda. Photo by Jean Biziman for Gates Foundation One area, and perhaps the most important area, where this cooperation matters is language. There are thousands of languages spoken in Africa. But much of the technology used to develop AI relies on data in widely spoken languages (in many cases in Africa, English and French), leaving many African languages underrepresented. This limits who can use these tools and how useful they can be. For a young person who speaks an African language but struggles with English or French, AI may not offer the same opportunities it offers someone who is fluent in these languages. The Masakhane research community is working to address this problem by developing natural language processing technologies for African languages. The community consists of Africans representing different languages across Africa. It is an example of what can happen when African researchers collaborate to make technology more inclusive. Through initiatives such as the Masakhane AI Languages Hub, researchers can develop datasets across 40 African languages to support the creation of more useful AI tools. In the 2026 Goalkeepers Report , Bill Gates said AI must b e able to work in every language spoken to create significant equality. Goalkeepers 2026 Report African countries can build on this work by investing in shared language resources, supporting local researchers and making datasets available for responsible use. Instead of each country working independently on similar challenges, regional partnerships could help researchers share knowledge and develop tools that serve communities across borders. item.content:encoded: Photo source: Goalkeepers 2026 Report For years, Africans have explored how to connect seamlessly without hurdles. As several opportunities are being explored through AI, Africans are also exploring whether AI can be used to advance cross-country opportunities and equity. If it can, what would it look like? What are the initial challenges that can hinder it from happening? What can governments and organisations do to enhance it? Artificial intelligence is changing how people learn, work, build businesses and access information. For young Africans, what opportunities does it present to solve problems, develop new skills and participate in an economy that is becoming increasingly digital? How can those opportunities be available to everyone in the same way? A young person with reliable internet access, a laptop and access to AI training has an advantage over someone who lacks these resources. The gap widens further when we consider young people across countries with different levels of digital infrastructure and investment. If AI is to improve the lives of African youth, access to its benefits must extend beyond the countries and communities already positioned to take advantage of it. African countries need to work together, share resources and invest in solutions that respond to the needs of their people. Bill Gates in Rwanda. Photo by Jean Biziman for Gates Foundation One area, and perhaps the most important area, where this cooperation matters is language. There are thousands of languages spoken in Africa. But much of the technology used to develop AI relies on data in widely spoken languages (in many cases in Africa, English and French), leaving many African languages underrepresented. This limits who can use these tools and how useful they can be. For a young person who speaks an African language but struggles with English or French, AI may not offer the same opportunities it offers someone who is fluent in these languages. The Masakhane research community is working to address this problem by developing natural language processing technologies for African languages. The community consists of Africans representing different languages across Africa. It is an example of what can happen when African researchers collaborate to make technology more inclusive. Through initiatives such as the Masakhane AI Languages Hub, researchers can develop datasets across 40 African languages to support the creation of more useful AI tools. In the 2026 Goalkeepers Report , Bill Gates said AI must b e able to work in every language spoken to create significant equality. Goalkeepers 2026 Report African countries can build on this work by investing in shared language resources, supporting local researchers and making datasets available for responsible use. Instead of each country working independently on similar challenges, regional partnerships could help researchers share knowledge and develop tools that serve communities across borders. This could make it easier for young Africans to access educational resources, health information and other services in languages they understand. AI can also help make opportunities available to people outside major cities. In agriculture, for example, PlantVillage Nuru uses a smartphone camera and AI to help farmers identify crop diseases. The application can work offline, making it useful in areas where internet connectivity is limited. Although the tool does not remove every challenge farmers face, it demonstrates how AI can make certain kinds of technical knowledge more accessible. Solutions like this could benefit young farmers and agricultural entrepreneurs across Africa. Countries facing similar agricultural problems could collaborate to test, adapt and improve existing tools instead of developing separate solutions from the beginning. Universities, research institutions and governments could support these efforts by sharing expertise and investing in technologies that respond to local conditions. African countries can work together to create more opportunities for young people to learn AI skills, participate in research, access mentorship and build businesses. Regional programmes could connect students with employers and investors across borders, allowing talent to find opportunities beyond national job markets. They could also help young people learn from one another and develop solutions that can be adapted to different African communities. Bill Gates in Rwanda. Photo by Jean Biziman for Gates Foundation. These efforts must be supported by investments in electricity, affordable internet, devices and digital education. Without these basics, AI training and other opportunities may continue to reach those who already have the most access. Governments and technology companies must also protect users’ data, address bias and ensure that the development of AI does not exclude women, people with disabilities or young people in rural communities. The African Union’s Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy , endorsed in 2024, provides a basis for countries to pursue a more coordinated approach to AI development. The challenge now is to translate that ambition into practical opportunities for young people. Africa does not have to approach every AI challenge as a separate national problem. By sharing knowledge, supporting local innovation and opening more pathways to education and employment, countries can make their investments go further. Success should not be measured only by the number of AI tools developed or the amount of money invested in the technology. It should also be measured by whether a young person, regardless of where they live, has a fair chance to use AI to improve their life. This will be part of the conversation centred around this year’s Goalkeepers 2026 . After hosting engaging and immersive events in the Nordics and New York, Goalkeepers is coming to Dakar on October 29 for the event, “Equitable AI and the Future of African Youth.” The post How Can Africans Advance Cross-Country Equity and Opportunities Through AI? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
item.description: Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining It’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”. The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading. Continue reading...

item.title: Lise Klaveness: ‘Certainly there are people that can challenge Infantino’
item.description: Norwegian federation president distances self from Fifa presidency but believes governing body can be reformed As the rain whips around Oslo’s government quarter, Lise Klaveness is shielding herself from the wind, trying to work out tactics. “Of course we cannot probably do everything alone, but we have a voice, we have the right to speak, we have the right to suggest, so let’s see,” she says. “We will at least try to be a spearhead.” The president of the Norwegian Football Federation wants to re-engage Fifa, and other governing bodies, on the topic of remedy. A slightly arcane aspect of human rights policy in normal times, the importance of remedy became very clear in the aftermath of the World Cup in Qatar, when the families of those injured or killed in the work that led up to the tournament were left without financial compensation after Fifa chose to direct a legacy fund elsewhere. Continue reading...

item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Sid Lowe
item.content:encoded: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

item.title: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment Sign up for our free newsletter here And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager . Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth , coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it. But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically ? This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Continue reading...

item.title: Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans
item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest. Continue reading...

item.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
item.description: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

There were lots of moments like that. Continue reading...

item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
item.description: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price. The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors . item.title: Star Trails
item.description: This long-duration image shows star trails above Earth and the blue lights of fishing boats and the yellow lights of Indonesian cities stretching below the International Space Station as it orbited 258 miles above the Banda Sea.

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. Continue reading...

item.title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera
item.description: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold . The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices. Continue reading...

item.title: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable
item.description: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera Google’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse. The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year. Screen: 6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12 or 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm Weight: 204g Continue reading...

item.title: Superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
item.description: N44 is a complex nebula filled with glowing hydrogen gas, dark lanes of dust, massive stars, and many populations of stars of different ages. One of its most distinctive features, however, is the dark, starry gap called a “superbubble,” visible in this Hubble Space Telescope image in the upper central region.
item.content:encoded: N44 is a complex nebula filled with glowing hydrogen gas, dark lanes of dust, massive stars, and many populations of stars of different ages. One of its most distinctive features, however, is the dark, starry gap called a “superbubble,” visible in this Hubble Space Telescope image in the upper central region.

item.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
item.description: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight.

item.title: Igniting Roman's Journey
item.description: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

item.title: August Lunar Eclipse Rises Over Louisiana
item.description: A lunar eclipse is visible over southern Louisiana. The lunar eclipse was visible throughout much of North and South America and part of Europe and Africa between Aug. 27-28. The Full Moon slipped through Earth’s shadow on Aug. 27, continuing into Aug. 28 for some parts of the world, resulting in the lunar eclipse. At maximum eclipse, the Moon takes on a dramatic dark, ruddy or coppery tint along the covered edge. New Orleans is home to NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility, where stages for NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and structures for Orion spacecraft are produced for the Artemis missions.

item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Artemis III RS-25 Engine Processing: #3 Lift
item.description: Technicians prepare to transfer the #2 RS-25 SLS (Space Launch System) rocket engine (front) to the work stand with the #3 engine (back) for integration with the Artemis III core stage rocket on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During Artemis III, the four RS‑25 engines will launch the Orion spacecraft and its crew of four into low Earth orbit, generating more than two million pounds of thrust at liftoff.

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
